_note: Archaeological, traditional, and museum sites tied to the biblical narrative — not per-person memorials (most biblical figures have no confirmed burial site; see CLAUDE.md). `identification` distinguishes archaeologically confirmed site identifications from traditional or disputed ones; this must stay visible on the map itself, not just in body text.

places.name: Jericho (Tell es-Sultan)
places.identification_note: Tell es-Sultan is confidently identified as biblical Jericho. What remains disputed is not the site itself but how its excavated destruction layers correlate with the conquest narrative of Joshua 6 — a dating question tied to the wider early-date/late-date Exodus debate, not a site-identification question.
places.description: One of the oldest continuously inhabited sites in the world, and the city whose walls fell before Israel in Joshua's conquest narrative.

places.name: Capernaum
places.identification_note: Excavated remains on the Sea of Galilee's north shore, including a fourth-century synagogue built over an earlier one, are confidently identified as Capernaum.
places.description: Peter's hometown and the base of much of Jesus's Galilean ministry; a first-century house identified by early Christian tradition as Peter's own has been excavated beneath a later church.

places.name: Tel Megiddo
places.identification_note: A UNESCO World Heritage tell with confidently identified stratified remains spanning the biblical period.
places.description: A strategic fortress city controlling the Jezreel Valley, mentioned repeatedly in the historical books and the source of the name Armageddon (Har Megiddo) in Revelation.

places.name: Masada
places.identification_note: Confidently identified from Josephus's first-century account and matching excavated remains.
places.description: Herod the Great's clifftop fortress above the Dead Sea, later the site of the Jewish rebels' last stand against Rome in AD 73 — Second Temple-era history that forms the backdrop to the New Testament world rather than a site Scripture itself narrates.

places.name: Ancient Corinth
places.identification_note: Extensively excavated, including the bema (judgment seat) where Paul was likely brought before the proconsul Gallio.
places.description: A major Roman commercial city where Paul spent eighteen months planting a church and later wrote two of his most substantial letters.

places.name: Ephesus
places.identification_note: One of the best-preserved Roman cities in the eastern Mediterranean, including the theater where a riot broke out over Paul's preaching.
places.description: Home to the temple of Artemis, one of the ancient world's Seven Wonders, and to a church Paul spent three years establishing.

places.name: Areopagus (Mars Hill), Athens
places.identification_note: The rock outcropping below the Acropolis is confidently identified as the Areopagus of Acts 17.
places.description: Where Paul addressed Athenian philosophers, reasoning from an altar 'to an unknown god' to the resurrection of Christ.

places.name: Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
places.identification_note: Venerated since at least the second century as the birthplace of Christ, making it one of the oldest continuously attested traditions of its kind — but it remains a tradition, not an archaeologically provable location, since the Gospels give no coordinates beyond 'Bethlehem.'
places.description: Built over a grotto traditionally venerated as the site of Jesus's birth.

places.name: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum
places.identification_note: A museum holding, not a site-identification question — the Dead Sea Scrolls it houses are themselves confidently authenticated.
places.description: Houses the Dead Sea Scrolls, including the great Isaiah scroll — the oldest known copies of large portions of the Hebrew Bible, over a thousand years older than previously known manuscripts.

places.name: Tomb of the Patriarchs (Cave of Machpelah), Hebron
places.identification_note: A continuous, well-documented tradition since antiquity identifies this site as the cave Abraham purchased from Ephron the Hittite. It is one of the stronger traditional identifications in the region, but — like all such sites — is tradition rather than archaeological proof, since the cave itself has not been excavated (it lies beneath an active place of worship).
places.description: Traditionally the burial place of Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, and Jacob.

places.name: Traditional Tomb of David, Mount Zion
places.identification_note: A medieval tradition, not attested before the Crusader period. Most archaeologists doubt this location matches David's actual burial in the City of David to the south (1 Kings 2:10), where his tomb has never been definitively located. Included here as the well-known traditional/pilgrimage site, clearly distinguished from the biblical text's own claim.
places.description: A medieval pilgrimage site venerated as David's tomb, though most scholars place his actual burial elsewhere in the older City of David.

places.name: Garden Tomb, Jerusalem
places.identification_note: One of two competing candidate sites for Jesus's burial and resurrection, proposed in the 19th century. Included alongside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre rather than in place of it, since the two traditions compete and this site does not silently take a side.
places.description: A rock-cut tomb near a skull-shaped rock outcropping, proposed as an alternative resurrection site to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

places.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
places.identification_note: The traditional site venerated by most Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, and other ancient churches since the fourth century, when Constantine's builders identified it beneath a pagan temple. The oldest and most widely held tradition, though — like the Garden Tomb — not something Scripture itself pinpoints with certainty.
places.description: Traditionally venerated since the fourth century as the site of both the crucifixion (Golgotha) and the resurrection.
